source: Li and Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice (FSE)
finding: Professional debugging is a four-step loop: reproduce, build and update a mental model, work on a fix, validate the fix. Most time goes to the mental model step.
numbers: 12 individuals (7 professionals, 5 live-streamers), 17 debugging tasks, about 10.9 hours (7.8 h on 11 tasks plus 3.1 h on 6 tasks). Mean time: 12% reproduce, 57% mental model, 13% fix, 18% validate. Four unfinished sessions all ended in the mental model step.
limits: Participants had to be able to show their code, so the sample is not random. Sessions were arranged in advance. Some observations began after debugging had started or ended before the bug was fixed.
agent_relevance: S2 should be a running model that the agent spends most of its budget on, not a one-off summary. About half the effort goes to evidence gathering, not to patching.

source: Li and Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice (FSE)
finding: The mental model has two parts: what the developer believes they do not know (uncertainty) and what they guess may be happening (speculation). Developers update uncertainty with factual evidence first, then speculate on that base.
numbers: All developers tracked uncertainty on all tasks (qualitative coding of think-aloud). Example: after DevTools showed data stored correctly, S4 asked where it is returned, then added a console log at that point.
quote: the goal is to learn the least about the codebase to fix the issue
limits: Qualitative grounded theory. No effect sizes. Coding is by the two authors.
agent_relevance: S2 can hold two explicit lists: known facts (with source) and open unknowns, plus a separate list of loose speculations. A guardrail can require each speculation to name the evidence that would settle it.

source: Li and Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice (FSE)
finding: Developers rarely state testable hypotheses. They hold vague speculations and refine them as evidence arrives. This may explain why interviews say 'scientific method' while observation shows other behaviour.
numbers: Qualitative finding. For contrast, a performance-bug study cited in the paper counted scientific hypothesis testing in only 79 fifteen-second instances versus 832 instances of inspecting source.
limits: Different tasks and methods. The contrast study had all participants on one bug, so it does not generalise well.
agent_relevance: Do not force a formal hypothesis at every step. A cheap running list of unknowns plus cheap checks may match what experts do. Formal hypotheses suit expensive tests.

source: Li and Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice (FSE)
finding: Developers practise knowledge avoidance: they build a breadth-first, good-enough model and skip tactics that need deep learning. This contradicts advice to first learn the system thoroughly.
numbers: P1 spent 52 minutes finding which change introduced the bug, 12 minutes looking for earlier fixes, and 13 minutes reproducing at a different scope, instead of studying the faulty logic. Others used AI help, asked experts, or applied temporary DOM fixes.
quote: developers often aim to construct a "good-enough" mental model that allows them to move forward
limits: Single research group, small N, mostly web apps. Several participants had under 50% familiarity with their code.
agent_relevance: S2 should include a cost check on each learning step: the cheapest way to cut the search space (history, bisect, ask, narrower repro) before reading deeply.

source: Li and Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice (FSE)
finding: Evidence comes from two tracing modes. Forward tracing follows execution from a known state. Backward tracing starts at the failure and works back, often through version history. Which mode dominates depends on familiarity.
numbers: Seven of eight participants used forward tracing. Backward tracing was primary only for P1 (under 5% familiar with a very large codebase); P3 and P4 (under 20% familiar) used it as a secondary mode. P2 and P5 (about 50% or more familiar) used it less. Navigation combined with execution was nearly universal, with two exceptions.
limits: Eight to twelve people. Familiarity is self-reported. Counts per mode are small.
agent_relevance: Give the agent both operators: coarse backward narrowing when the repo is unfamiliar, fine forward tracing once the region is known.

source: Li and Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice (FSE)
finding: Developers go beyond code. They use version control history, colleagues, web resources and AI as evidence sources to update the model, more than earlier studies reported.
numbers: Qualitative: external resources appear in most sessions. No percentages given in the text read.
limits: Self-selected professionals who could share their screens. Streamers are a different population.
agent_relevance: Evidence gathering for S2 should list non-code sources the agent can reach (git log and blame, issue tracker, docs, search) and tag each observation with its source.

source: Li and Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice (FSE)
finding: Simple bugs can be fixed without running the code. For complex bugs developers turn to execution to check speculations.
numbers: P5 fixed task A by reading only; on tasks B and C P5 alternated reading and running. S5 spent a 2-hour session switching between reading and breakpoints.
limits: Anecdotal within a small sample. Complexity was judged by the developers themselves.
agent_relevance: Trigger rule for the agent: read first for simple, local issues; escalate to execution (logs, debugger, test) when speculations multiply or the path crosses modules.

source: Ko, Myers, Coblenz, Aung (2006) An Exploratory Study of How Developers Seek, Relate, and Collect Relevant Information during Software Maintenance Tasks (TSE 32(12))
finding: Developers working on unfamiliar code search, relate and collect information of perceived relevance. Success depends on clear cues from the environment and a way to keep what was found. The model draws on information foraging theory.
numbers: 31 developers recruited; analysis on the 10 most experienced in Java (7 self-described experts, 3 above average). 70 minutes, 5 maintenance tasks (2 debugging, 3 enhancement) in Eclipse. Average 3.4 (SD 0.8) tasks finished. Interruptions took 22% (SD 6) of time and were excluded.
quote: searching, relating, and collecting information of perceived relevance
limits: Lab study, small program, unfamiliar code, 10 analysed people. Authors say the program was much smaller than industrial code.
agent_relevance: The cue-and-collect model maps to S2: the agent needs a store for collected relevant locations (a working set) so it does not rediscover them.

source: Ko, Myers, Coblenz, Aung (2006) An Exploratory Study of How Developers Seek, Relate, and Collect Relevant Information during Software Maintenance Tasks (TSE 32(12))
finding: Navigation overhead was large and failed searches began with misleading cues. Developers lose track of code they already found.
numbers: 35% of non-interrupted time (average 19 minutes) went to navigating between code fragments. In the debugging tasks 88% (SD 11) of searches led to nothing later useful. About 25 (SD 9) minutes, around 36% of time, went to inspecting irrelevant code. Eight of nine who tried the SCROLL task searched for 'paint' and landed on a method that was not the cause.
limits: One small Java app. A generic file name held the real bug while a suggestive class name misled half of developers on the YELLOW task.
agent_relevance: Expect LLM agents to fail the same way: the first guess from surface names is often wrong. Keep a record of rejected locations and add a 'what else explains the symptom' step.

source: Ko, Myers, Coblenz, Aung (2006) An Exploratory Study of How Developers Seek, Relate, and Collect Relevant Information during Software Maintenance Tasks (TSE 32(12))
finding: Division of labour in maintenance tasks: reading, editing, searching and navigating, and testing each took a fifth or less to a quarter of the time.
numbers: About a fifth reading code, a fifth editing, a quarter on textual search and dependency navigation, a tenth testing the app, 5% (SD 2) switching between tools, 6% (SD 4) reading API docs.
limits: Lab times for 10 people with Eclipse. Only 2 of 5 tasks were debugging.
agent_relevance: Baseline for budgeting: humans spend little time testing in the lab, so an agent that runs tests often behaves differently and may gain from it.

source: Ko and Myers (2004) Designing the Whyline: A Debugging Interface for Asking Questions about Program Behavior (CHI)
finding: Interrogative debugging: programmers naturally ask 'why did' and 'why didn't' questions. Half of errors in Alice came from false assumptions in the hypotheses they formed while debugging.
numbers: From the authors' earlier Alice studies: 50% of all errors due to false assumptions; 68% of questions were why-didn't; 85% about a single object; why-didn't questions were asked only about code that could plausibly have run.
limits: Alice is a novice 3D environment. Numbers come from the authors' own prior studies cited in the paper.
agent_relevance: For S2: store the visible symptom as a question ('why did X not happen') and answer it by looking for the first failed predicate, not by guessing code regions.

source: Ko and Myers (2004) Designing the Whyline: A Debugging Interface for Asking Questions about Program Behavior (CHI)
finding: The Whyline let programmers ask those questions directly and see runtime-based answers. It cut diagnosis time and raised tasks completed.
numbers: Six matched debugging scenarios: time to diagnosis fell by an average factor of 7.8 (repeated measures ANOVA F(1,5)=12.64, p<.02). In 90 minutes the With group (5 participants) finished M=3.20 tasks (SD .457) versus M=2.25 (SD .500) for the Without group (4 participants), t(7)=3.0, p<.02, a 40% increase. The Whyline was useful for 19 of 24 questions.
limits: Nine participants in total, HCI master's students, one prototype environment, scenarios matched after the fact. Not a randomised same-bug design.
agent_relevance: A tool that answers 'why' from a recorded trace beat guessing. A trace or log of execution makes S2 questions answerable by lookup.

source: Ko and Myers (2008) Debugging Reinvented: Asking and Answering Why and Why Not Questions about Program Behavior (ICSE)
finding: Java Whyline: novices with the tool beat experts without it. Experts with the tool still speculated about a cause first, then looked for a matching question.
numbers: Whyline group of 9 pilot participants: median 4 minutes (range 1-12) versus 18 self-described expert Java developers with Eclipse: median 10 minutes (range 3-38), p<.05 Wilcoxon rank sums. Unpublished follow-up: experts with the Whyline were twice as successful in half the time on ArgoUML bugs. Initial developer guesses were wrong almost 90% of the time (cited from earlier studies).
quote: the novices in our pilot study tended to outperform the experts
limits: One task (a colour slider bug), small pilot, control data from a different earlier study with interruptions removed. Authors flag limited generality. The follow-up is unpublished and preliminary.
agent_relevance: Speculation before evidence is a trap even for experts. The agent should state the symptom question first and let evidence propose causes, rather than guess a cause and look for confirmation.

source: Wyrich et al. (2023) Source Code Comprehension: A Contemporary Definition and Conceptual Model for Empirical Investigation (history of Brooks, Letovsky, Pennington, Littman, von Mayrhauser; secondary account)
finding: Brooks (1978, 1983) top-down theory: understanding is successive refinement of hypotheses about the program, guided by beacons such as names and comments. Soloway and Ehrlich (1984) added programming plans and rules of discourse that help experienced developers.
numbers: Historical account; no new data. Cited results: Adelson found experts recall larger semantic chunks; Wiedenbeck (two experiments) found beacons help experienced, not inexperienced, developers.
limits: Secondary source (a 2023 review under review). Primary papers are not open access, so numbers come from the review.
agent_relevance: Beacons suggest the agent should weight identifier names and comments as cues but verify them (Ko found misleading names cost about 36% of time).

source: Wyrich et al. (2023) Source Code Comprehension: A Contemporary Definition and Conceptual Model for Empirical Investigation (history of Brooks, Letovsky, Pennington, Littman, von Mayrhauser; secondary account)
finding: Letovsky (1987), from think-aloud protocols, describes a knowledge-based understander: a knowledge base, an evolving mental model, and an assimilation process. The understander is an opportunistic processor using top-down and bottom-up cues. The model has specification, implementation, and annotation (links between them).
numbers: Verbal protocols from six professional developers adding a feature while thinking aloud. Recurring events: asking questions and making conjectures with levels of certainty.
limits: Six people, 1980s study, secondary account. Certainty was coded, not measured.
agent_relevance: Direct template for S2: goals (spec), code facts (implementation), and links (annotation), each with a certainty tag. Matches the question and speculation lists in Li and Coblenz.

source: Wyrich et al. (2023) Source Code Comprehension: A Contemporary Definition and Conceptual Model for Empirical Investigation (history of Brooks, Letovsky, Pennington, Littman, von Mayrhauser; secondary account)
finding: Pennington (1987) separated the program model (control flow and operations) from the situation model (data flow and goal hierarchy), borrowed from text comprehension. Experts first built control-flow structure; functional knowledge came later.
numbers: From the review: study 1 found procedural units, not functional units, formed the basis of expert representations; study 2 on longer programs found control-flow understanding preceded function understanding. A web record says study 1 tested 80 professional programmers (not opened).
limits: Secondary account only. The original paper (Cognitive Psychology 19(3):295-341) and the DTIC report returned HTTP 403.
agent_relevance: Order of construction: structure first, purpose later. The agent could trace control flow before inferring goals and fill the situation model once a task gives a reason.

source: Wyrich et al. (2023) Source Code Comprehension: A Contemporary Definition and Conceptual Model for Empirical Investigation (history of Brooks, Letovsky, Pennington, Littman, von Mayrhauser; secondary account)
finding: Littman et al. (1986) split mental models into static knowledge (what components do) and causal knowledge (how they interact during execution). Having both is a strong mental model. Systematic strategy (trace data flow between routines) beat as-needed strategy in their account.
numbers: Review text: some developers used a systematic strategy and some an as-needed strategy; those using the systematic strategy did better. Sample size and success counts were not given in the text read.
limits: Secondary account. Original sample size and counts not verified.
agent_relevance: Static plus causal: keep both a map (what exists) and an execution story (what happens in order). Map-only models are weak.

source: Wyrich et al. (2023) Source Code Comprehension: A Contemporary Definition and Conceptual Model for Empirical Investigation (history of Brooks, Letovsky, Pennington, Littman, von Mayrhauser; secondary account)
finding: Von Mayrhauser and Vans (1995) integrated metamodel joins the top-down model, Pennington's program and situation models, and a shared knowledge base; developers switch between them. Gilmore argues that debugging is a loop that contains comprehension, not a separate step after a finished model.
numbers: Review text: the metamodel incorporates Brooks, Letovsky, Shneiderman and Mayer. Gilmore: bugs deeper in the program structure were found more easily, suggesting detection during an ongoing comprehension process.
quote: comprehension is part of a larger debugging loop
limits: Secondary account. The metamodel is descriptive; it is not a computational model that predicts behaviour.
agent_relevance: Supports interleaving S2 (model update) with testing, not strict phases. Matches Li and Coblenz, where developers return to the model step after a failed fix.

source: Burkhardt, Detienne, Wiedenbeck (1997) Mental Representations Constructed by Experts and Novices in Object-Oriented Program Comprehension (Interact)
finding: Extension of Pennington's two-level theory to object-oriented code. The situation model was better developed than the program model even early in comprehension, which differs from Pennington's procedural results.
numbers: 30 OO experts and 21 OO novices read a library program for a documentation or reuse task. Situation versus program model: M=4.36 vs 3.55 of 6, F(1,43)=110.94, p<.0001. Situation scores rose from phase 1 (4.17) to phase 2 (4.55), F=10.83, p<.002; program model did not change. Experts beat novices on situation model (4.56 vs 4.10, F(1,44)=19.17, p<.0001) but not on program model.
limits: Boundary condition: the order of model building depends on paradigm (OO versus procedural). Question-based measure, one program, English and French speakers, small lab study.
agent_relevance: Whether to start from structure or purpose depends on code style. For OO repos, class and relation maps come early and carry most of the expert advantage.

source: Burkhardt, Detienne, Wiedenbeck (1997) Mental Representations Constructed by Experts and Novices in Object-Oriented Program Comprehension (Interact)
finding: Static knowledge (objects, relations, goals) was better than dynamic knowledge (client-server links, data flow). Experts led only on static knowledge.
numbers: Static M=4.74 (SD .68) vs dynamic M=3.62 (SD .96), F(1,45)=106.20, p<.0001. Experts 5.00 vs novices 4.36 on static, F(1,46)=34.23, p<.0001; no expert-novice difference on dynamic. Dynamic improved with phase (3.38 to 3.85, p<.0037).
limits: Same small study. Questionnaire recall and recognition, not live debugging.
agent_relevance: Dynamic (causal) knowledge is the hard part for everyone, so tools that supply traces (Whyline, execution logs) fill the weakest part of S2.

source: Chen et al. (2025) LocAgent: Graph-Guided LLM Agents for Code Localization
finding: LocAgent turns a repository into a directed graph of files, classes, functions, imports, invocations and inheritance, and lets an agent search it. This is an explicit, queryable system model for an LLM.
numbers: Abstract: fine-tuned Qwen-2.5-Coder-Instruct-32B reaches up to 92.7% file-level localization on SWE-Bench-Lite at about 86% lower cost than proprietary models; downstream issue resolution up 12% at Pass@10. On Loc-Bench file Acc@5: LocAgent (Claude-3.5) 83.39 vs Agentless 67.50, OpenHands 79.82, SWE-agent 77.68, CodeRankEmbed 74.29.
limits: Authors' own benchmark (Loc-Bench) plus SWE-Bench-Lite. Fine-tuning used Claude-3.5 trajectories. Table columns were read from PDF text and could be misaligned.
agent_relevance: A graph-shaped S2 beat text-only agents on localization. Evidence that building a structural model helps; worth testing in our harness.

source: Chen et al. (2025) LocAgent: Graph-Guided LLM Agents for Code Localization
finding: Better localization raised repair success, but only modestly.
numbers: SWE-bench-Lite repair: Agentless with Claude-3.5 localization Acc@5 58.39, Pass@1 26.31, Pass@10 33.58; LocAgent Claude-3.5 Acc@5 73.36, Pass@1 27.92, Pass@10 37.59; fine-tuned Qwen2.5-32B Acc@5 69.34, Pass@1 26.79, Pass@10 36.13.
limits: A 15-point localization gain gave a 1.6-point Pass@1 gain, so localization is not the only bottleneck. One benchmark.
agent_relevance: Do not invest in model-building alone; the fix and validation states also limit success.

source: Yu et al. (2025) OrcaLoca: An LLM Agent Framework for Software Issue Localization (ICML)
finding: OrcaLoca adds priority-scheduled actions, relevance scoring, and distance-aware context pruning based on a code graph. It treats exploration as scheduling and shrinks context by graph distance.
numbers: New open-source best function match rate of 65.33% on SWE-bench Lite; raises the resolved rate of an open-source framework by 6.33 points. Across leaderboard submissions only 53.5% of issues get a correct function match on average. SWE-bench repos average 3,010 files and about 438K lines.
limits: Leaderboard-style comparison; framework differences confound. Only abstract and introduction numbers were checked; ablation tables were not read.
agent_relevance: Pruning context by graph distance is a concrete way to keep S2 small as the repository grows.

source: Samir and Rahman (2026) Improved Bug Localization with AI Agents Leveraging Hypothesis and Dynamic Cognition (CogniGent, ICPC)
finding: CogniGent copies human debugging: restructure the report, filter candidates, generate hypotheses, investigate them by walking the call graph depth-first, and have an observer check them. It outperformed the baselines.
numbers: 591 bug reports from 15 systems (Bench4BL extended, 132 versions). MAP gains of 23.33-38.57% at document and method level and MRR gains of 25.14-53.74% over baselines. Best variant (Devstral): document MAP 0.407, MRR 0.418, HIT@1 0.374, HIT@5 0.475, HIT@10 0.526. Method-level MAP 0.226.
limits: Localization from bug reports, not full repair. Open models (Devstral, Qwen-Coder, LLaMA). Baselines were run by the authors.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis steps helped localization on this benchmark, a counterpoint to the human finding that explicit hypotheses are rare.

source: Samir and Rahman (2026) Improved Bug Localization with AI Agents Leveraging Hypothesis and Dynamic Cognition (CogniGent, ICPC)
finding: Ablation: hypothesis generation and hypothesis testing carry most of the gain; restructuring and the observer add smaller steady gains.
numbers: Document/method MAP: full 0.407/0.226; one ablated variant each at 0.382/0.212, 0.364/0.189, 0.379/0.195, 0.360/0.183, 0.392/0.216 (restructuring, filtering, hypothesis, investigation, observer removed in that column order). The authors state hypothesis generation and testing give up to 19%.
limits: Row-to-component assignment is read from layout text with the marks lost, so it is inferred from column order. Check the table before citing.
agent_relevance: Test both formal hypotheses and looser speculation lists in our schema, since LLM agents and humans may differ.

source: Meta FAIR CodeGen Team (2025) CWM: An Open-Weights LLM for Research on Code Generation with World Models
finding: CWM is a 32B model mid-trained on Python execution traces and agent trajectories in Docker environments, so it models what code does at runtime. It is a trained world model of execution.
numbers: Over 120 M traced Python functions; ForagerAgent data about 3 M trajectories from 10.2k images and 3.15k repos. SWE-bench Verified pass@1 53.9% (65.8% with test-time scaling, best@16); LiveCodeBench-v5 68.6%; CruxEval-Output 94.3%.
limits: Terminal-Bench accuracy was only 26.3%. Trace prediction tested on small Python functions. Single lab report.
agent_relevance: Training on traces gave a stronger runtime model. Our scaffold has no training, so it needs real runs (logs, traces) to supply the same dynamic knowledge.

source: Meta FAIR CodeGen Team (2025) CWM: An Open-Weights LLM for Research on Code Generation with World Models
finding: Mid-training ablation: execution traces improve output and input prediction but not SWE-bench trajectory fit; only the agentic ForagerAgent data improved agentic SWE-bench measures.
numbers: Adding trace data significantly improved CruxEval-input and -output but left SWE-bench-Verified metrics unaffected; adding ForagerAgent data improved agentic SBV NLLs and added another 3.7% pass@1.
limits: Single lab, 32B model, numbers parsed from PDF layout.
agent_relevance: Knowing how code executes is not the same as knowing how to explore a repo; S2 needs both the execution model and the search habit.
